Migration is the movement of people from one place to another with the intention of settling temporarily or permanently in a new location. It can be internal (within a country) or international (between countries).  
Key causes of migration include economic factors (search for jobs and higher wages), social factors (better education, healthcare, or family reunification), political factors (war, persecution, lack of rights), and environmental factors (natural disasters, drought, climate change).  
Consequences of migration affect both origin and destination areas. Places of origin may experience population decline, loss of working-age people, and “brain drain,” but also receive remittances from migrants. Destination areas may gain labor, cultural diversity, and economic growth, but can also face pressure on services (housing, schools, hospitals) and social tension if integration is weak. Good planning and inclusive policies can maximize the benefits and reduce problems for both sending and receiving regions.  

12.  
Urbanization is the increasing proportion of a country’s population living in towns and cities. It usually occurs when people move from rural to urban areas in search of better opportunities.  
Causes of urbanization include industrialization (factories and services concentrating in cities), better job prospects, higher wages, more developed transport and communication, and access to education and healthcare. In some cases, rural poverty, landlessness, or environmental degradation push people out of the countryside.  
Impacts of rapid urbanization include the growth of informal settlements or slums, traffic congestion, pollution, unemployment or underemployment, and strain on water supply, sanitation, and public services. However, cities can also be centers of innovation, cultural life, and economic growth. Managing urbanization requires planning for affordable housing, public transport, green spaces, adequate infrastructure, and policies that reduce inequality between rural and urban areas.
